intro: A mixture is caught at one moment, as numbers or as a box of particles you can count. Calculate Q, compare it with K, say which way the reaction goes, then choose the justification that earns the point on a free-response question.
howItWorksTitle: Q, K and the justification readers want
howItWorks:
Q has the same form as K, using the amounts right now.

  • Q < K: too few products. The reaction proceeds forward until Q rises to K.
  • Q > K: too many products. The reaction proceeds in reverse until Q falls to K.
  • Q = K: at equilibrium. Forward and reverse rates are equal; no net change.

Solids and pure liquids are left out of Q and K. A justification earns the point when it states Q and K, compares them, and gives the direction that brings Q to K. The size of K alone, or a rate argument without Q, does not.

In a particle picture, turn each count into a concentration first. Q counts within 3% of the exact value.
